content.thinking:
I need to write this whole module in a single pass without testing, so I'll be extra careful with API usage. I'm designing a chunky Warcraft-style dwarf rifleman, about 1.3m tall, with huge shoulders, a big head and hands, short legs, a braided beard, and a blunderbuss with a flared muzzle, aiming for a hand-painted look using gradients, countershading, grain, and mottling.

I'm working out the full skeleton proportions now: hip and spine joint heights, head size and helmet height to total 1.3m, shoulder width and pauldron sizes, then arm segment lengths and a reasonable rest pose, probably an A-pose rather than full T-pose given the character needs to hold the gun.

For the gun, I'm deciding the right hand should grip it with the weapon carried diagonally across the body at hip level, pointing forward and slightly up, while the left arm stays in a simpler A-pose to avoid overlapping the gun model.

Checking the left arm's reach for gripping the barrel, I realize the proportions are too long for dwarf-scaled arms, so I'm repositioning the left hand closer along the barrel to keep the forearm length realistic.

Instead I'll simplify: just use a one-handed right-arm grip on the gun, with the left arm relaxed at the side holding a small powder horn prop, avoiding the awkward two-hand reach problem entirely.

I'm now computing the right arm's joint positions explicitly—shoulder, elbow, wrist—checking that each bone segment length stays consistent so the gun ends up resting naturally in the hand.

Working out the gun's local coordinate frame...

Now I'm working out the blunderbuss geometry itself — stock, grip, brass lock plate with hammer, trigger guard, and the barrel flaring into a bell-shaped muzzle, planning to build the flared section as a swept shape with a radius profile widening toward the end.

Still writing sweep/lathe code...

Now thinking through the arm rig: a bone chain with points for shoulder, elbow, and wrist, where the tip joint becomes the hand since a hand is defined as the tip of its arm chain.

For hands I'm planning finger geometry: fist spheres with box-shaped finger segments wrapped around the grip, deciding whether to add actual joints for digits or keep it simple given time constraints. I'll settle on a modest approach — each hand gets a small helper that builds finger chains (three fingers plus thumb) attached to the wrist joint.

Figuring out joint coordinates for the body: hips, pelvis, and legs with hip, knee, and ankle positions chained together as short polylines for each leg.

I'll go with catmull for the smoother corners either way, since the knots land at the same points. For the boots, I'm designing them as separate parts attached to the ankle bone -- a rounded box or lofted shape for the foot, with stations defining width and height at the ankle position.

Still writing boot loft stations...

I'm assigning the shaft to the knee-ankle bone since that span owns the shin geometry, with the foot attached at the ankle tip joint—rest pose can stay straight-ish for now. Moving on to the torso, I'm planning a barrel-chested dwarf build using a loft along a spine chain starting at the hips.

Writing spine chain code...

Caps are placed to stay hidden between head/neck and legs. I'm adjusting station positions and widths to add a slight forward belly shift, tweaking the hip, waist, and chest coordinates for a more natural torso curve.

Now I'm defining the shoulder pauldrons as large spheres positioned on the first arm joints, with the arm chains rooted at the shoulder and parented to the chest. I'm also setting up a short, thick neck chain connecting the chest to the head joint, with coordinates placed to keep the head properly aligned above the torso.

Since this is a single-shot reply with no further tool calls, I should avoid ambiguous local-coordinate helpers and instead work directly with explicit model-space coordinates for each bone, defining fixed center points like the head's position manually.

For the dwarf's head I'm shaping a broad skull with a scaled sphere, then painting ruddy cheeks and warm skin tones with noise-based variation, and building the signature braided beard as a loft of wide shapes sweeping down from the chin.

Still writing beard and braid placement logic...

I can compute position and tangent directly along the path myself, then pass those as explicit position and direction to each part, so orientation follows the curve naturally. For the braid links, I'll alternate ellipsoid segments with slight lateral offsets to mimic a plaited pattern, tilting each one's roll for visual variation.

For the facial detail, I'm layering small spheres for the eyes: a pale sclera, an ice-blue iris, a dark pupil, and a tiny highlight dot, positioned close together to sit deep under the heavy brow like a dwarven face.

Now I'm adding thick ginger brow bars as rods angled upward, a big bulbous ruddy nose with a bridge capsule, sweeping mustache curves that taper from thick at the nose down to thin where they merge into the beard, ruddy cheek spheres, and I'm about to shape the pointed ears.

I'm also considering adding a small stubby pipe tucked into one mouth corner for character, and I'm setting up the jaw as a separate joint-driven part so the lower jaw and attached beard mass can move independently from the skull.

For the mouth itself, I'm placing a tiny dark cavity between the mustache and beard to suggest an open mouth, mostly hidden by hair, with a subtle reddish flattened sphere marking the lip line. Now I'm turning to the helmet design, thinking through a rounded steel dwarf cap, possibly with a brass trim or nose guard rather than horns.

Working out the lathe profile for the dome, riveted rim, chin strap, and side flaps, defining the radial points that shape the bowl and positioning it over the skull so the rim sits just above the brow line.

I need to resolve a height conflict: the skull sphere's top reaches 1.275 but the eyes and brow sit lower, so I'm repositioning eyes to y=1.13, brow to 1.16, and the helm rim to 1.19, checking that the skull radius at that height (~0.137) stays under the helm rim radius (0.165). With the dome adding another 0.2 in height, the total model height comes out to about 1.39.

Since a dwarf should stand roughly 1-1.4m, I'm trimming the helm height down to 0.17 so the top lands near 1.355-1.38 with a spike or crest, which fits comfortably within the acceptable range. I'm defining the helm's lathe profile as a series of radius/height points forming a closed loop from the axis out along the base, up the outer curve, and back to the axis at the top, using 14 smooth segments, and I'm adding a rim band detail to finish the shape.

Adding rim torus ring...

Still working out the helmet dome geometry...

Checking the elliptical curve against my profile values, then adding a steel ridge with rivets along the edge. I'm also considering adding small horns or wing details to fit the dwarf helm aesthetic.

Adding curved brass-tipped horns sweeping up and outward from the helm sides for a heroic silhouette. I'm skipping a nasal guard since it'd clutter the nose area, opting instead for a brow plate detail.

For facial hair, I'm skipping the chin strap and cheek flaps as mostly hidden, and lofting the beard shape with jaw-bone stations that taper from wide at the chin down to narrow at the bottom.

I'm checking that the beard's depth slightly overlaps the chest geometry, which is fine since it gives the beard a natural protruding look over the chest. For coloring, I'm planning a ginger-to-pale gradient with vertical noise streaks to simulate hair grain.

Adding tuft scatter details...

Now planning braided beard sections—two side braids from chin height curving down to brass clasps with tassels, built from chained link spheres, maybe a small central braid too.

For the chest, I'm leaning toward a rugged dwarven rifleman look: leather vest, bandolier with powder flasks, shoulder plates, big buckled belt. Settling the palette around tan leathers, steel blue-grey, royal blue cloth with gold trim, brass accents, ruddy skin tone, and a ginger beard color, avoiding faction emblems.

Writing the paint shader logic...

Checking texel density for the paint atlas, estimating around 2mm per texel given a 1024px width over roughly 3 square meters of painted surface, so I may bump the atlas to 2048 or 4096 for sharper detail.

I'm also mindful of the 64 flat-color limit — paints don't count against it, but flat color strings do, so I'll cap the palette around 40 flat colors and reserve paints for large surfaces. Defining color constants now: steel, steel dark, brass, brass dark, wood, leather, and more.

For the gun stock I'm applying a wood grain paint with directional axis parameters using a vector type for grain direction, aiming for a realistic hand-painted wood texture.

Now I'm working out the gun's position relative to the hand, tracing the arm geometry from shoulder to elbow to wrist so the weapon sits naturally in the grip, computing coordinates for the pauldron, upper arm, and forearm segments.

Then I'm setting the gun's origin at the hand center and figuring its orientation, angling the barrel slightly forward and inward so it points across the body, while placing the butt behind the hand at an offset distance.

Checking the butt placement against the hip and thigh geometry to confirm there's no intersection with the elbow or arm, then laying out the barrel from grip to muzzle with a slight upward taper and flare at the tip -- noting the total weapon length comes out quite long.

Now I'm working out the left arm as a simple hanging A-pose, computing shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions and checking the segment lengths match natural proportions, then thinking about what the left hand should be holding -- maybe a flask or tankard rather than leaving it empty.

For the right hand gripping the gun, I'm planning to build the fist from knuckle capsules and finger chains, working out coordinates relative to the gun's grip axis so the fingers wrap realistically around it.

Still working out finger geometry...

Still placing the finger joints...

Now I'm adding bracers and cuffs at the wrists using torus shapes aligned to the forearm axis, attached to the elbow-to-wrist bone chain.

For the torso, I'm thinking through the blue jerkin design — a leather chest with steel pauldrons, painted with darker blue wool, lighter trim at the edges, and a central front lacing line down the chest.

For the brass buttons, instead of calculating coordinates by hand, I'll use a ray-casting approach against the torso surface to find front hits at each height, then place button parts directly at those points.

For the belt, I'm planning to cut a loop around the waist near the spine joint using the surface's loop function, then sweep that path with a belt cross-section to form the leather geometry.

Since the loop is planar and the tangent stays horizontal, the normal remains up throughout, so I can set the ellipse radii with vertical half-width larger than the radial thickness to get a wide, flat strap. I'm considering using a box section instead for sharper, hard-surface edges typical of a belt.

For placement, I need to make sure the belt sweep only follows the torso surface and doesn't get distorted by the arms crossing near that height — restricting the surface target to the torso mesh handles that. Then I'm positioning the buckle and pouches: a brass plate at the front, and hip pouches offset to the sides based on the torso's width at that height.

I'm also designing a curved powder horn as a tapered sweep with a brass cap, and planning a diagonal bandolier strap that drapes around the torso as a closed loop — sketching out the front, hip, and back anchor points for that path now.

Actually a simpler, safer approach: make it a round cord bandolier using a tube sweep with radius .022, then attach small cylindrical cartridges perpendicular to the path by sampling points along the draped curve with position and tangent.

Rather than orienting cartridges upright like spikes, I think flat short cylinders (like brass discs or caps) sitting along the strap would read better as decorative studs, or alternatively small pouch boxes stuck with their local axis following the surface normal.

I'll orient these pouches using the strap's tangent direction as the flow parameter, giving leather pouches with brass caps running along the bandolier. I'll skip any chest emblem and instead consider armor pieces -- a riveted steel gorget, blue jerkin, leather straps, and layered dome-shaped steel pauldrons for the shoulders.

For the pauldron, I'm defining a lathe profile that creates a domed plate oriented outward and slightly upward along the arm, positioned to sit just over the shoulder joint.

I'll paint it steel with a brass trim torus around the rim and a small brass spike cone on top, then scatter a ring of tiny brass rivet spheres around the edge for detail. For extra character, I'm considering adding a backpack with a rolled bedroll and cookpot to give this rifleman figure a lived-in, adventurous feel.

Still placing backpack and strap details...

For the neck, I'm adding a steel gorget collar as a torus ring sitting above the chest, accounting for how the loft geometry's dome cap extends beyond the torso's rounded top station.

That rounded cap would actually poke up too high, intruding into the head region, so I'm switching the torso loft to use flat caps instead, keeping the chest top flat so pauldrons and the collar can cleanly cover the transition, with the pelvis handled as its own separate loft section.

Checking the shoulder and armpit geometry now — the pauldron spheres bridge the gap between the narrower torso and wider arm placement, and the upper arm radius tucks in close enough to touch the torso side without a visible seam, so that joint should read fine.

For the hip region, I'm adding a pelvis sphere scaled to fill the gap between the legs, parented to the hips bone, colored to match the pants so there's no bare gap showing between the leg chains.

Everything feels too flat and hard-edged right now, so I want to add a tabard or loincloth flap hanging from the belt down to the knees — extruding a thin cloth-like outline with gold trim at the belt front to break up the silhouette and add some softness.

I'm positioning the leather apron with studs just outside the belt, letting it hang down over the thighs with a slight tilt for a natural drape, going stylized Warcraft-style with just a front tabard and small back flap, using a zigzag hem and painted trim detail.

Now I'm working out the knee pads and caps — brass pads at the knee joint with a steel kneecap and rivets, sitting rigidly on the knee bone. I'm also setting up the leg naming convention so left is positive x and right is negative, then sketching out the thigh proportions from hip to knee to ankle.

I need to pin down leg thickness values, hip joint placement under the hips root, and how the foot/ankle tip joint resolves from a three-joint chain when the typed tip is null, falling back to the last joint index. I'm also cataloging the joint role names across chains — leg, arm, spine, neck, head, jaw — to standardize the bone metadata options.

Now I'm sketching the neck chain with two points, parenting the head joint off the neck's tip joint, and adding a jaw joint aimed outward from the head; I'm also considering whether beard braids need their own joint chains for hanging motion.

For the braids, I'm planning small curved chains of three or four points each (tagged with a loose "tail" role) parented to the jaw, giving each side a few named links so they can swing naturally.

Tallying up the full joint budget — spine, neck, head, jaw, legs, arms, fingers, and now braids — I'm staying comfortably under the 160 bone limit.

Now I'm designing the skin paint function with ruddy cheeks and nose coloring based on position relative to the head center, using noise for subtle stubble texture and smoothstep/mix blending. Writing the hand-painted helper...

Still writing shading logic...

Writing tuft texture SVG...

For orientation, I'm figuring out the hair should have a wide base at the bottom and taper to a tip at top, with the flow direction pointing downward so the strands lean along the surface like a hanging beard.

Now I'm thinking through the mustache geometry: curved sweeps of ginger paint that flow out from under the nose and curl upward at the tips, tapering in thickness, anchored to the head bone near the jaw.

I'm also placing the eyes, nose, brow, and cheeks along the skull surface, calculating protrusion depths so the nose tip and eyes sit just forward of the scalp curve, then working out how the beard and sideburns loft from the helmet down the face sides to join at the chin for that enclosed-face look.

Small ear spheres sit tucked behind the sideburns near the jaw, and I'm checking that the brow bar height clears just under the helmet rim so nothing clips. Then I'm stacking up the total head height from chin to helmet ridge and stud, landing near 1.39, and weighing whether that fits the target dwarf proportion of roughly 1 to 1.4 overall.

I settle on tightening the helmet dome height to about 0.165, pushing the rim to 1.19 and the ridge to about 1.37, confirming the dome interior fully covers the skull top and that the face stays visible beneath the rim line. Now I'm shifting to the gun model, sketching out a loft profile for a curved flintlock-style stock with butt, heel, and width/height stations defined in the gun's local coordinate space.

Writing stock loft stations...

Thinking about where the hand fist sphere sits relative to the stock, with the barrel positioned above the fore-end around y=+0.07 for z beyond 0.1, while the wrist/stock center stays lower near y=0.01 at z=0.

I'm continuing to map out the stock stations along the z-axis, checking where the wood forend top meets the barrel's underside so the wood cradles the barrel properly through the forend, which ends around z=.30. Then I'm checking the hand grip position at the origin, sizing the hand sphere radius against the stock cross-section there.

Now I'm shifting to the barrel itself: defining the main cylindrical sweep from G(0,0.075,-0.06) to G(0,0.075,0.52) at radius .03, then adding a flared bell section near the muzzle with a smoothly increasing radius array, capping it with a dark interior disk to suggest the bore, and coloring the barrel steel blue-grey. I'm adding brass ring details -- a few bands along the barrel plus a brass lip ring at the muzzle -- to give it a more finished, decorated look.

Now I'm working out the lock mechanism and trigger assembly for the flintlock: a brass lock plate on the outer side, a curved cock/hammer piece swept from the lock toward the pan, a small brass pan box, a steel trigger rod extending down from near the breech, and a trigger guard built as a curved brass sweep arcing around where the hand grips, making sure the guard geometry stays close to where the fingers wrap near the origin.

Realizing the hand and trigger guard were overlapping, I'm repositioning things so the lock, hammer, and trigger guard sit forward of the wrist grip rather than directly at the hand's position, with the barrel breech starting just behind the hammer. I'm laying out a clearer set of z-coordinates along the stock -- from the butt through the wrist grip to the forward lock area and muzzle -- to keep all these parts properly spaced.

Adjusting the decal plane placement...

Now thinking through the ramrod: a thin rod running under the barrel near the forend, plus brass thimble rings to hold it in place.

For the muzzle, I want a decorative brass band with a ring of small studs circling the bell, computed using perpendicular offset vectors around the barrel's centerline — I'll build a helper function to generate these ring positions. Next I should move on to larger accessory pieces like a powder horn, pouches, flask, and hammer.

I'm setting up a local coordinate frame for the gun: defining a direction vector along the barrel, an up vector orthogonal to it, and a cross vector for left/right, so I can place boxes, cylinders, and toruses consistently oriented along the gun's axis using these basis vectors as their local x/y/z.

For the arm, I'm deciding on a simple paint scheme—tan linen sleeve on the upper arm transitioning to bare skin with a steel bracer at the forearm—implemented as a single swept tube with color bands switching partway through the sweep near the elbow joint.

Legs get brown wool pants swept as one tube, with boots on the lower shin including a rolled-over cuff detail at the top using a small torus shape.

Still adding boot details...

I'll give the sole a separate flatter dark loft hugging the bottom of the foot, slightly wider than the boot itself, then move on to setting the hands to skin tone.

Now I'm choosing hair colors: ginger base with a lighter streak and darker roots, and picking a ruddy skin tone. For the tabard, I'm figuring out where the front panel hangs below the belt, interpolating station heights and depths at the belly to estimate its front projection and accounting for belt thickness.

Positioning the tabard's z-depth and hem length against the pelvis and thigh geometry, tilting it slightly forward so the bottom hem drapes naturally against the body rather than floating away from it.

Now I'm shaping the tabard outline into a pointed banner with a sharp tip at the bottom, then coloring it blue with a gold border and center stripe by checking distance from the edges to decide border versus fill regions.

Now I'm placing belt pouches: a leather box with flap on the left hip for powder/ammo, hanging below the belt line with brass stud detail, and starting the powder horn as a curved sweep from the belt using spline points.

I'm sizing the horn with tapered radius and banding colors, brass caps at the tip, then shifting to the backpack — a boxy leather pack attached at the chest bone, positioned to sit against the torso's back curvature.

Rather than a plain box I'm considering an extrude-with-bevel approach for a chunkier, more rounded pack shape, sketching a helper for beveled slab shapes.

Then I'm sketching the actual pack: a bevelled box with a lid flap, straps and brass buckles, plus a bedroll cylinder laid across the top for extra detail.

Adding more pack details...

Straps attach to the spine bone via smooth skin weights, skipping the gun strap idea. Now I'm sketching the torso paint logic: blue base with a v-neck, gold lacing down the center, and conditional trim near the hem, building this as a nested paint function that returns either gold or the base jerkin color depending on position.

I'm deciding to add a button row along the center seam with a darker painted line rather than crisscross lacing, plus a lighter chest panel and subtle belly shading inherited from the base skin, before moving on to pants paint for the pelvis and legs and detailing on the pauldrons.

For the head, I'm considering a brass earring torus and possibly a small pipe with a bezier stem running from the mouth out to a bowl, though I note it might intersect with the mustache geometry and could just be skipped for simplicity given the part count is already around 250.

Working out the facial feature placements now: mustache sitting just under the nose without clashing, and eyes using recessed sclera spheres with small iris discs offset toward the front for depth.

Adding ice-blue irises with dark pupils and tiny glints, plus heavy brow ridges positioned so they overlap the eyelid tops slightly for that heavy-lidded dwarf look. Moving on to sizing a prominent nose next.

Still working through API details...

Skipping toes for now. I'm working out the boot loft geometry — placing the heel and toe stations so the rounded caps extend to the right back/front offsets without making the boots too oversized for the dwarf's proportions.

Still writing station widths...

For the sole I'll handle it inline in the boot paint function rather than a separate loft, darkening any vertex below a certain height to look like a sole, nested inside the broader body paint logic. The loft sides will just use the default low-poly circle resolution, then I'll move on to the hips.

For the beard, I'm layering a grain texture for hair streaks, then gradienting that between a base ginger color and lighter tips near the top of the beard, nesting the paint functions so the gradient wraps the grain pattern.

Now I'm generalizing the shading helper to accept any color input—resolving it through the paint system first, then deriving lighter and darker variants via mix based on a light direction constant.

Writing shading function...

Defining material color constants...

I realize geometries shouldn't be shared across parts since baking may write per-vertex colors or UVs, so I should create a fresh geometry for each part instead—defining a small helper to generate sphere geometries on demand.

Now setting up the imports for the builder, math, path, and paint utilities, deciding against using the glow kit since nothing in this piece (iris, brass, fuse) really calls for it. I'll skip glow to avoid unused imports and move on to defining the meta object with name, description, and style tags.

Then I start building the dwarf rifleman model: initializing the builder and a seeded random generator, deciding to keep palette colors at module scope but create paints and textures inside the build function since SVG textures may need the document context. I begin laying out the skeleton, starting with the hips as the root joint and building a spine chain using a Catmull-Rom curve through several points, parenting it to the hips and naming the segments spine1, spine2, and chest.

I continue defining the neck as a short polyline chain parented to the chest joint, with a thick rod mesh covering it since the neck will largely be hidden by a beard. From there I set up the head joint oriented upward with a slight forward tilt, and the jaw joint aimed outward from the head using a target point. Then I move to lofting the torso geometry, feeding in station points through a sweep with flat caps, parented to the spine bone and colored with the jerkin palette, while thinking through how the sweep frame should stay oriented along the vertical path.

Now I'm building the pelvis as a scaled sphere part bound to the hips joint, and then looping over both left and right sides to construct the legs: each is a chain running from hip to knee to ankle using catmull interpolation, parented to the hips with named joints and a contact point near the foot. I'm sweeping a tapered radius profile along each leg for the pants mesh, then adding a boot shaft as a rod from the ankle partway up toward the knee with its own radius taper and boot coloring, plus a cuff torus at the top of the shaft, while working out which joint to bind the boot bone to and how the sweep caps should behave at the ankle tip.

Now I'm adding scaled, color-tinted kneepad spheres positioned just in front of each knee, deciding to skip thigh straps and greaves for now, then moving on to defining the arms. I'm laying out shoulder, elbow, and wrist points separately for the left and right sides, building catmull chains named by joint per side, sweeping tapered arm radii with a color band split between sleeve and skin fabric that I'm adjusting to avoid landing right at the elbow joint, and adding a rolled sleeve cuff as a torus oriented along the forearm direction near that color boundary.

Now I'm adding a tapered steel bracer cylinder with brass rim torus accents at both ends along the forearm, plus a bone for the elbow joint, then moving to hand placement — computing palm sphere positions by offsetting from the wrist along the normalized forearm direction, working out the exact unit vector for the right arm so the hand and eventual gun origin align consistently with the body.

Checking the gun's butt and muzzle placement relative to the hand and hip: using the gun direction vector offset from the hand position, the butt lands roughly beside the hip below the elbow height, which checks out, while the muzzle extends far forward and upward — confirming the gun passes naturally through the gripping hand as the forearm angles down and forward.

For the fingers wrapping the stock, I need to reconsider the grip geometry since the stock's wrist axis runs horizontal along the gun direction, so the fingers actually form rings in the cross-sectional plane perpendicular to that axis rather than along it, each ring offset slightly in z and wrapping from the outer side of the hand around to the inner palm side.

Placing the palm sphere scaled outward to wrap the outer side of the stock, with fingers curling underneath. For the left hand, I'll mirror this with the palm offset outward and fingers hanging down from the front of the palm.

Working out left hand coordinates: wrist, elbow, and a direction vector give me the palm center position, then I'm laying out finger base points in a row offset along z with slight inward curl, followed by the thumb base.

I'm skipping the gloves/gauntlet detail for now and defining the head center point. For hair, I'm sweeping sideburn curves down each side of the skull using catmull-rom paths with tapering radii, checking they partially overlap the skull surface as intended, and now moving on to lofting a beard shape along the jawline.

Defining more beard stations...

I'm reconsidering the beard length against the belt and thinking about adding braids hanging from the cheeks for a more "braided beard" dwarf look. I'll shorten the main bib to around y .72-.84 and let three separate braids extend further down to around y .62, giving it that distinct layered dwarf style.

Working out braid geometry with gold rings, brass clasps, and tasseled tuft ends...

I'm checking whether the beard occludes jerkin buttons—it covers the chest from y .84 to 1.07 while buttons sit partially visible below, which is fine. I also need to decide braid joint parenting: should they follow the jaw bone so they swing naturally when the mouth opens, or stay rigid on the neck?

Now I'm working out the braid chain geometry—sampling points along a catmull-rom curve for each strand, offsetting link positions laterally in alternating directions, and elongating each link sphere along the tangent direction with slight scale distortion, while alternating between two hair color tones for visual variation.

Still planning accessories: brass tie rings at the base and tip of each braid, terminal beads with tufted hair sprays, beard card placement on the bib, and mustache sweeps rigged to the head bone. Now shifting focus to the helm's horns, band, and stud placement along the rim height.

Working out the helm geometry: centering it over the skull with the rim radius positioned so the front edge clears the brow bars, then lathing the outline around that axis with steel coloring, bone-rigged to the head. Adding decorative brass elements -- a brow band torus, a secondary mid-band ring, and a ring of small brass stud spheres spaced around the rim.

Now I'm designing the ridge crest as a swept catmull curve with steel-dark coloring and brass tips, and working out the horn geometry as bezier curves rising from the sides of the helm with tapered radii, bone-cream coloring with grain texture, and brass sleeve bands near their base.

I'm thinking about whether to add ear flaps to the helm sides, deciding to skip them, and planning ginger eyebrow rods instead. Then I shift to the beard cards -- scattering hit points across the beard surface with minimum distance and normal-based filtering, setting flow and lean parameters, and starting to draft an SVG texture for individual beard strand cards.

Writing SVG strand paths...

Then I move on to designing a gold scroll engraving decal for the stock, starting another SVG texture.

Positioning the scroll texture plane on the correct face and checking orientation for both the left and right sides of the barrel...

I'm also sizing the stock's side plane width against the box's tapered geometry near z=-0.2, checking the half-width and y-span against the stock's center and height to keep within tolerance.

Next I'm attaching gun parts to the wristR bone, planning the brass lock plate etching, and considering extras like belt buckle and whether to add a glow effect before writing out the full structure carefully.

Setting up geometry helper functions...

Positioning the pauldron dome over the shoulder joint with a slight tilt and offset, then adding a smaller secondary dome over the upper arm for a tiered armor look, plus plate rings as accents.

Now I'm adding trim details: a brass torus ring around the dome's rim, a spiked cone boss on top aligned with the shoulder axis, and a circular array of eight rivets positioned at a set radius and height, which requires computing perpendicular basis vectors for the axis to place them evenly around the ring.

For color, I'm leaning toward a steel-blue enamel plate with brass trim for a heroic, Alliance-style look, keeping it logo-free and relying purely on the color palette.

Settling on brown leather jerkin with dark blue wool sleeves as the single accent color, steel pauldrons, and deciding where else blue shows up—tabard, helm cloth—while picking a reddish-brown for the bedroll.

Locking in blue as the recurring accent across tabard, sleeves, and bedroll stripes, with dark brown pants and boots, steel-and-brass pauldrons with a gold spike, and a ginger beard for warmth. Now I'm cataloguing the exact hex strings I'll need for each material—brass, dark leather, iron, and eye colors—to keep the palette consistent in code.

Setting up the builder with a precomputed skin paint using a base ruddy tone and highlight/shadow variants, then building a face paint function that calculates cheek positions relative to the head for blush shading.

Defining steel material texture...

Defining more material paints...

Still defining horn and helm colors...

Still defining torso loft...

Still defining paint regions...

I need to reconsider the orientation frame for the belt loop's cross-section — figuring out how the up-vector rotates as the tangent direction sweeps around the loop, since tangent direction determines whether +Z points up or down for the ribbon's radial thickness.

For the belt cross-section, I'll use a constant ellipse radius function returning the half-extents for the sweep rather than a box shape to avoid sharp corners.

For the buckle, I'm casting a ray into the torso to find the front surface point, then placing a thin brass plate box there oriented so it flows outward along the surface normal, with a null-check helper to grab front-surface hits safely.

For the belt studs, I'm walking along the belt path at intervals and placing small brass spheres offset radially outward from the loop, using the nearest surface point to approximate the outward direction rather than assuming a perfect circle.

For the bandolier, I'm draping a closed catmull-rom path around the body and sweeping a leather tube along it, then plan to add pouches spaced along part of that strap.

Still writing placement logic...

Still writing extrude params...

Now I'm planning the gun-building function and starting to draft the full file, including a steel gorget ring around the neck using a torus shape positioned at the chest/collar area.

I'm working out skull geometry and positioning next: eye sockets placed symmetrically around the skull center, the skull itself as a scaled sphere, and the lower jaw as a smaller scaled sphere attached to the jaw bone with facial coloring.
